---
title: "Showing the Distance on the Display"
unit: 3
cluster: "Building a Distance Meter"
---

A reading is most useful where we can see it, without a computer attached.
With the sensor and the display on the same board, a program can measure
the distance and show it on the display, making a **distance meter**.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

- show the distance on the display, as it changes
- write a new reading over the old one, so no old characters are left
- warn with a blinking sign when something comes too close

## Showing the distance

There is no new wiring: we use the circuit with both the display and the
sensor. Plug in the USB cable, connect Thonny to the board, and type this
program in the editor:

```python
from machine import I2C, Pin, time_pulse_us
from machine_i2c_lcd import I2cLcd
import time

i2c = I2C(0, sda=Pin(4), scl=Pin(5), freq=100000)
lcd = I2cLcd(i2c, 39, 2, 16)
trig = Pin(19, Pin.OUT)
echo = Pin(18, Pin.IN)

lcd.clear()

while True:
    trig.on()
    time.sleep_us(10)
    trig.off()
    duration = time_pulse_us(echo, 1, 30000)
    if duration < 0:
        line = "Out of range"
    else:
        line = "Distance: " + str(round(duration / 58)) + " cm"
    lcd.move_to(0, 0)
    lcd.putstr(line + " " * (16 - len(line)))
    time.sleep(0.5)
```

The measurement is the one that printed the distance in the Shell. Instead
of printing, the program now makes a line of text, and writes it on the
first line of the display.

The display keeps every character until something is written over it. Say
the first reading is `Distance: 120 cm`, which fills all 16 places, and the
next is `Distance: 9 cm`, two characters shorter. Written on its own, the
new line covers only the first 14 places, and the display shows
`Distance: 9 cmcm`. So the program adds spaces to the end of each line:
`16 - len(line)` is the number of places the line leaves empty, and
`" " * (16 - len(line))` is that many spaces. Each line then covers all 16
places, and nothing of the old one is left.

The program could call `lcd.clear()` each time round the loop instead, but
that blanks the display for a moment before each new reading, and the
display flickers.

Click Run, and hold a hand in front of the sensor. The display shows the
distance to it, and changes twice a second as the hand moves. Take the hand
away, and point the sensor at an open space, and it shows `Out of range`.

## Warning when too close

The second line is free for a warning. The program blinks the warning sign we
drew earlier, and `Too close!`, while something is
closer than a limit. Change the program to:

```python
from machine import I2C, Pin, time_pulse_us
from machine_i2c_lcd import I2cLcd
import time

i2c = I2C(0, sda=Pin(4), scl=Pin(5), freq=100000)
lcd = I2cLcd(i2c, 39, 2, 16)
trig = Pin(19, Pin.OUT)
echo = Pin(18, Pin.IN)

warning = bytearray([
    0b00100,
    0b01110,
    0b01010,
    0b11011,
    0b11111,
    0b11011,
    0b11111,
    0b00000,
])
lcd.custom_char(0, warning)
lcd.clear()

limit = 10

while True:
    trig.on()
    time.sleep_us(10)
    trig.off()
    duration = time_pulse_us(echo, 1, 30000)
    distance = round(duration / 58)
    if duration < 0:
        line = "Out of range"
    else:
        line = "Distance: " + str(distance) + " cm"
    lcd.move_to(0, 0)
    lcd.putstr(line + " " * (16 - len(line)))

    lcd.move_to(0, 1)
    if duration > 0 and distance < limit:
        lcd.putstr(chr(0) + " Too close!")
        time.sleep(0.25)
        lcd.move_to(0, 1)
        lcd.putstr(" " * 12)
        time.sleep(0.25)
    else:
        lcd.putstr(" " * 12)
        time.sleep(0.5)
```

`limit` is the distance in centimetres below which the warning blinks.
When something is closer, the program writes the sign and `Too close!`,
12 characters in all, waits a quarter of a second, writes 12 spaces over
them, and waits again: one blink. Otherwise, it writes the 12 spaces, so a
warning from an earlier time round the loop does not stay on the display.
Either way, the loop takes half a second, so the distance is still measured
twice a second.

The check `duration > 0` matters. When nothing is in range, `duration` is
negative, so `distance` is negative too, and a negative number is less than
10. Without the check, the warning would blink when there is nothing in
front of the sensor at all.

Click Run. The first line shows the distance, and the second is empty.
Bring a hand closer than 10 cm, and the warning blinks below the distance.
Change `limit`, and run the program again, to warn at a different distance.

## Summary

A program shows a changing reading by writing each new one over the old,
padded with spaces to the width of the line, and blinks a warning by
writing it and then spaces over it.

| Code | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `lcd.move_to(0, 0)`, then `lcd.putstr(line)`, each time round the loop | writes the new reading over the old one |
| A shorter line written over a longer one | leaves the end of the longer one on the display |
| `line + " " * (16 - len(line))` | pads the line with spaces to 16 characters, so it covers all of the old one |
| `lcd.clear()` each time round a loop | blanks the display before each reading, so it flickers |
| `if duration > 0 and distance < limit:` | is true only for a real reading closer than the limit |
| Text, a short sleep, spaces over the text, a short sleep | blinks the text once |
